The email address that was given was not even mine or one that I'd ever used in the past. In trying to obtain MY OWN report, I couldn't even remember the old phones I had years ago, ( which is one of their verification questions ) so I couldn't even get my own report to see if there was an inquiry on my report from XXXX XXXX. How's that for privacy? My identity was stolen in XX/XX/XXXX for someone that opened a XXXX account in my name. It was again the credit bureaus that released my credit history without my consent/authorization. The identity thief even gave them an address that I'd supposedly had in the most recent 2 years, that's not even in my profile as one of my addresses EVER! They should never have released my credit report to XXXX. That also allowed for my identity to be stolen. If the CREDIT BUREAUS were sanctioned for each and every instance that they fail to follow the law, identity theft would go down. But, NO ONE MAKES THEM ACCOUNTABLE FOR THIS. It's not fair to us as the consumer. What information is required of each creditor when they ask for a consumers report from the bureaus? Not to mention Equifax 's " not so long ago '' Breach, which could be the very way my name, ss # and dob was illegally obtained by whomever opened this account in my name with the very CREDIT REPORT RELEASED by Equifax. I take it nothing was done to the bureau for this breach and the consumers are still taking the hit for it. Equifax only requires that a credit supply them with the consumers name, ss # and date of birth and some bogus email address that was simply my XXXX. That doesn't appear to be compliance with the FCRA section 604. That's all the information that a creditor has to produce and the bureaus are allowed to just release your credit report? Any hospital that a consumer has been to, any procedure facility, any electricity carrier, any cable company, any mortgage company ALL have this information on every consumer in the world. That information is standard everywhere. The bureaus should require more information before simply releasing consumer reports based on that. Particularly when the creditor has received this information ONLINE. They have no idea who is on the other side of that computer and the bureau certainly doesn't. I feel that 95 % of fraud and identity theft could be prevented if the Big 3 Credit Bureaus ( and all the small ones ) were made to comply with the law!!!!!!

I never stated this.

Your letter states that there are undisputed transactions at the same merchant location/terminal with similar dollar amounts. 
Yes, I have made numerous withdrawals of money from the same ATM over the past years, but never six consecutive withdrawals at the same time. For example, if I walked down a street with money in my pocket and was robbed by a thief, I would go to the police and file a complaint. If I walked down that same street and was not robbed, I would have nothing to complain about. Right? 
Also, as soon as I was advised by Chase regarding the {$370.00} fraudulent transaction ( literally minutes after the six fraudulent transactions were posted ), I responded by answering NO to whether I made this transaction. So, Chase was aware that I was disputing the transaction. 
Yes, I didnt dispute the other five fraudulent transactions. Because I wasnt aware of them at the time. 
Then you go on to state that we are not able to prove fraud occurred. 
What? 
You already suspected fraud by asking whether I made the withdrawal on XX/XX/XXXX. ( See above. ) Why would anyone make six consecutive withdrawals moments after midnight? ( One of which was flagged by the Chase security system. ) I have never made more than one withdrawal in a day. Not six consecutive withdrawals in a few minutes! In fact, I thought that I wasnt allowed to do this? 
It seems that the only basis for your decision is that my password was used. In any case, you must be aware of scams that are employed to steal a customers password? I have heard that sometimes copies of an ATM transaction can be illegally made from an ATM machine. 
Why should I, a Chase customer for over 25 years with six accounts maintaining an average balance of at least {$150.00}, XXXX a month, be held solely responsible for this apparent fraud. 
THIS IS OUTRAGEOUS!

We will address your concerns about your customer service experience internally. We reviewed your claim numbers XXXX and XXXX on XX/XX/2023, for the ATM transactions totaling {$940.00}. The management of XXXX at XXXX XXXX informed me that I had two options. The first option was to pay two months of rent. The second option was to move-out, XXXX would put the apartment back on the market, and I would pay a reduced rent amount until the apartment was rented. 

As I contemplated, management informed me that the complex was XXXX % occupied, the apartment was their most desirable layout, with the addition of a private balcony, one of the best views, and there were not anymore like it that were available. She then recommended that I take the second option because she couldn't fathom that particular unit not being rented within a month. 

Based on the professional judgement of XXXX management I deferred to their perspective and chose to pay the reduced rent and allow them to put the apartment back on the market and pay the reduced rent until the apartment was rented. 
Within days of my conversation with XXXX management I returned to the office, on XX/XX/2014, to inform them of my departure and to return the keys. All the employees in the office were different from a few days before. I spoke to one of them. I was told the apartments had been sold, and were under new management. I mentioned my situation and was told that all was well and that all arrangements made with XXXX at XXXX XXXX would be honored.

I also informed her of the specific XXXX employee that told me my options for the early termination of the lease. I requested that she contact XXXX to verify and clarify the options and terms they had stipulated, and then call me back.

She told me that she had gotten in contact with XXXX and they confirmed the terms of my early lease termination as being : ( 1 ) I would vacate the apartment, ( 2 ) they would put the apartment back on the market, and ( 3 ) I would pay a reduced rent until the apartment was rented.

I asked whether they had been showing the apartment and whether there were any prospective renters showing interest in the apartment. She told me it was their responsibility to rent the apartment and it was my responsibility to pay the rent. The sudden shift of tone gave me an uneasy feeling that something was not right. I told her that I was at work and when my shift ended I would use the online web portal to make the payment.

I did a search of their website as a prospective renter utilizing the same method I originally employed to find and apply for the specific apartment unit I rented. I searched multiple ways, and although I was provided all the unit numbers of available apartments, my specific apartment number of XXXX was not listed. I told her that not putting the apartment on the market constituted a breach of the conditions of our agreement.

XXXX XXXX AND IQ DATA INTERNATIONAL ARE VIOLATING FEDERAL AND STATE LAWS OF EXTORTION AND THE XXXX XXXX AND XXXX XXXX ( XXXX ) ACT AND THE FAIR DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES ACT XXXX XXXX and IQ Data International are aware that I acted in accordance with terms established and imposed upon me before change of ownership. consumer_complaint_narrative:
On XX/XX/XXXX, I discovered a collections account with United Collection Service on my XXXX App. This account was recorded for XXXX XXXX XXXX at a time that I was not in XXXX XXXX. On XX/XX/XXXX, I sent a certified letter to UCS with three ( 3 ) mailings : ( 1 ) dispute of debt, ( 2 ) request for verification, ( 3 ) mail-only communication. Pursuant to FDCPA and Florida Law, UCS had five ( 5 ) days to respond to this, and they did not. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I called United Collection Service at or about XXXX P.M. and spoke with XXXX ( spelling may be incorrect ) regarding this issue. I was never provided a last name. I informed XXXX that United Collection Service did not provide a verification of debt, nor provide any form of written correspondence regarding this matter. XXXX confirmed that no written correspondence of any kind was ever issued in this matter from the beginning of the reporting of the alleged debt. Upon informing XXXX that under the Federal Trade Commission Act rules, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, United Collection Service had five ( 5 ) days to respond to my document requesting verification of debt by writing only and by mail only, she informed me that United Collection Service would not respond to mail requests for verification, which is in direct conflict with the rules outlined by the Federal Trade Commission Act, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. I then asked to speak with XXXX supervisor, and was transferred to someone named XXXX. Again, I did not receive a last name. I left a message on XXXX voicemail regarding this issue, but have not heard back. I have included a relevant timeline below. 

Under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ), consumers always have the right to request verification of a debt after finding out about the alleged debt in question within 30 days of the first written correspondence with the Collection agency. I notified United Collection Service on my first written correspondence with the company, thus the verification period has not been waived and has, in fact, been fully satisfied. Collection agencies such as United Collection Service are required to respond to these verifications within five ( 5 ) days of receipt of the request. At this time, I have received zero correspondence from United Collection Service regarding any contested matter. When I spoke with XXXX, she informed me that no mailing had gone out regarding this matter, and that it would not, because United Collection Service does not send out verifications as a response to written requests for verification. This is in direct conflict with the FTCA, FCRA, and FDCPA, all federal rules for conducting debt collection.

Because United Collection Service did not, and in fact refused, to furnish this consumer with a verification of debt within the statutorily required period, it is necessary that United Collection Service delete any and all debts being reported to any and all credit reporting agencies, as United Collection Service has not complied with, and refuses to comply with, the Federal Trade Commission Act, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and/or the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. At this time, United Collection Service has waived their right to contest and report this debt any further. Per my original mailing, United Collection Service may only contact me through written mail to discuss this issue.

Additionally, because UCS never sent any kind of mailing regarding this debt, as verified through their agent, XXXX, I was never informed of my ability to dispute, which is required under the law. To date, I have received nothing from UCS in regard to this debt.

consumer_complaint_narrative: I have never had a deals with with these company and never opened them. Somebody stolen my personal information. ( a ) Block. Except as otherwise provided in this section, a consumer reporting agency shall block the reporting of any information in the file of a consumer that the consumer identifies as information that resulted from an alleged identity theft, not later than 4 business days after the date of receipt by such agency of ( 1 ) appropriate proof of the identity of the consumer ; ( 2 ) a copy of an identity theft report ; ( 3 ) the identification of such information by the consumer ; and ( 4 ) a statement by the consumer that the information is not information relating to any transaction by the consumer. ( b ) Notification. A consumer reporting agency shall promptly notify the furnisher of information identified by the consumer under subsection ( a ) of this section ( 1 ) that the information may be a result of identity theft ; ( 2 ) that an identity theft report has been filed ; ( 3 ) that a block has been requested under this section ; and ( 4 ) of the effective dates of the block. ( c ) Authority to decline or rescind. ( 1 ) In general. A consumer reporting agency may decline to block, or may rescind any block, of information relating to a consumer under this section, if the consumer reporting agency reasonably determines that ( A ) the information was blocked in error or a block was requested by the consumer in error ; ( B ) the information was blocked, or a block was requested by the consumer, on the basis of a material misrepresentation of fact by the consumer relevant to the request to block ; or ( C ) the consumer obtained possession of goods, services, or money as a result of the blocked transaction or transactions. ( 2 ) Notification to consumer. If a block of information is declined or rescinded under this subsection, the affected consumer shall be notified promptly, in the same manner as consumers are notified of the reinsertion of information under section 1681i ( a ) ( 5 ) ( B ) of this title. ( 3 ) Significance of block. For purposes of this subsection, if a consumer reporting agency rescinds a block, the presence of information in the file of a consumer prior to the blocking of such information is not evidence of whether the consumer knew or should have known that the consumer obtained possession of any goods, services, or money as a result of the block. ( d ) Exception for resellers. ( 1 ) No reseller file. This section shall not apply to a consumer reporting agency, if the consumer reporting agency ( A ) is a reseller ; ( B ) is not, at the time of the request of the consumer under subsection ( a ) of this section, otherwise furnishing or reselling a consumer report concerning the information identified by the consumer ; and ( C ) informs the consumer, by any means, that the consumer may report the identity theft to the Bureau to obtain consumer information regarding identity theft. ( 2 ) Reseller with file. The sole obligation of the consumer reporting agency under this section, with regard to any request of a consumer under this section, shall be to block the consumer report maintained by the consumer reporting agency from any subsequent use, if ( A ) the consumer, in accordance with the provisions of subsection ( a ) of this section, identifies, to a consumer reporting agency, information in the file of the consumer that resulted from identity theft ; and ( B ) the consumer reporting agency is a reseller of the identified information. ( 3 ) Notice. In carrying out its obligation under paragraph ( 2 ), the reseller shall promptly provide a notice to the consumer of the decision to block the file. Such notice shall contain the name, address, and telephone number of each consumer reporting agency from which the consumer information was obtained for resale. ( e ) Exception for verification companies. The provisions of this section do not apply to a check services company, acting as such, which issues authorizations for the purpose of approving or processing negotiable instruments, electronic fund transfers, or similar methods of payments, except that, beginning 4 business days after receipt of information described in paragraphs ( 1 ) through ( 3 ) of subsection ( a ) of this section, a check services company shall not report to a national consumer reporting agency described in section 1681a ( p ) of this title, any information identified in the subject identity theft report as resulting from identity theft. ( f ) Access to blocked information by law enforcement agencies. No provision of this section shall be construed as requiring a consumer reporting agency to prevent a Federal, State, or local law enforcement agency from accessing blocked information in a consumer file to which the agency could otherwise obtain access under this subchapter.

consumer_complaint_narrative:
Here 's a chronological description of what happened. On the morning of Saturday, XX/XX/XXXX, I got a call from someone in Chase Bank 's fraud/security office telling me that some suspicious-looking activity had shown up on my debit card. She very quickly went through a list of these charges, around 15 or 20 in total, asking if I recognized them. Most of them I didn't. And most of these unrecognized transactions were payments to XXXX  for around {$15.00}, though a few were bigger, including the largest payment for {$210.00} to a cell-phone company that I don't use. I told her that these charges were indeed fraudulent and thanked her for catching them. She reassured me that we wouldn't be held responsible for this activity. Chase would proceed with its usual investigation, she said, and reimburse our account in the meantime. She also said she'd cancel my obviously compromised debit card and have a new one sent in the mail. I felt reassured.

On the morning of XX/XX/XXXX, I went through my online list of recent activity and noticed that one unfamiliar charge, for around {$56.00}, had been missed. This transaction was to another cell-phone company that isn't ours for a purchase we didn't make. So I called the Chase Customer Claims office and asked that this charge be added to the list of fraudulent ones. It was in this conversation that I first noticed a Chase employee treating me with suspicion. It didn't help that our phone connection was bad ( or that I'm hard of hearing ). Every Chase employee since then has treated me and my wife with a strong measure of defensiveness, obviously seeing us as having done something wrong.

My new debit card arrived in the mailbox on Saturday the XX/XX/XXXX. On Sunday I tried to activate it by phone but, strangely, got an automated message saying that the card was already active. On Monday morning I went into a local branch office here in XXXX XXXX XXXX, at XXXX XXXX XXXX, and asked a teller to activate the card. He told me that the card had been reported stolen and that I should destroy it and request another one.

I was in a hurry that day but returned the next afternoon, Tuesday the XX/XX/XXXX. In the interim, my wife had tried to use her debit card ( linked to the same checking account ) and had it declined. On Tuesday two different bankers at the same branch location, one of them an assistant branch manager, informed me that our accounts had been completely frozen by the fraud/security department and that we could not withdraw any money from them -- not from the checking account that had been affected by the hacking, and not from our two different savings accounts. As of this morning, XX/XX/XXXX, we still have received nothing in writing to this effect. We're told that a letter was sent when the freezing took place, but if that's true it hasn't arrived.

We didn't have any holdings at any other bank. All of our cash and cash savings was inaccessible to us, with no real explanation and no timeline for resolution. I asked one of the bankers in the local branch if this response seemed as strange to him as it did to me. I've been lucky enough that none of my debit cards has ever been hacked before, but I know cases like this occur all the time. After talking on the phone to the fraud department, he told me, shrugging his shoulders and shaking his head, " No, it seems like they're looking into something else. '' We still don't know what that " something else '' is. On the morning of XX/XX/XXXX, we talked to three or four people after initially calling the Customer Claims hotline again. Finally my wife was able to speak to someone who stated, with more clarity, that a decision had been made to close all three of our accounts.

We still could not access any money in these accounts, she said, and could not come to receive a cashier 's check in person. Instead, in 7-10 business days, we should expect a check in the mail ( regular mail! ) in the amount of all of our balances, which will come to a total of just under {$90000.00}. And we are not allowed to open another account with Chase Bank now or in the future. The decision, this person declared to my wife, who was fighting back tears, is irreversible.

The only explanation provided was that too many " claims '' had been made on our account of late. The bank treated each of the fraudulent transactions as a separate claim, requiring a separate investigation, and I guess we can understand that 15-20 may seem like a high number. And yet they were all relatively small charges, most of them around {$15.00}, made over a span of a few days -- the time frame, obviously, when the debit card had been hacked. The total disputed amount comes to around {$500.00} : enough to make us want to resolve the problem and re-secure our accounts, sure, but not enough to make us think we were at risk of losing all our cash and savings. The bank 's reaction seems wildly disproportionate, which makes us assume that they've decided we are guilty of some greater misdeed that they haven't named. We can only conclude that they refuse to tell us anything substantial because they are still investigating us.

As of the evening of XX/XX/XXXX, our checking account, which had a balance of around {$8800.00}, and a small savings account for our XXXX-old daughter, which had a balance of {$8000.00}, had been XXXX out according to my Chase phone app. The previous balances had been subtracted for a " XXXX Check '' : I assume for the check we must hope to receive by mail. But at that point our savings account, with for us a sizeable balance of {$71000.00}, was still showing up as usual. We took screen shots to verify and can provide them as needed.

As of yesterday morning, though -- the morning of XX/XX/XXXX -- that large savings account no longer appeared at all in my online profile. I can not even locate the account history. It's as though the account, with all the cash we stowed away for several years as we prepared to have a child and then became new parents, had vanished overnight. We're told to expect this amount to come by check, in around 7-10 business days. In the meantime we are blocked from almost all the money we have in the world. We can use what little cash we happened to be carrying in our wallets, yes, and the money our parents can try to wire us, and our credit cards. And yet we still have bills to pay. And because our young daughter was diagnosed last month with XXXX XXXX XXXX, we have XXXX and equipment to buy.

product: Credit reporting, credit repair services, or other personal consumer reports
sub_issue: Credit inquiries on your report that you don't recognize
consumer_complaint_narrative:
On XX/XX/2020, I applied for a preapproval with Eagle Home Mortgage. I approved a credit pull, but only one. Instead, Eagle Home Mortgage pulled my XXXX  report, and then pulled a report for all bureaus, including XXXX. This resulted in XXXX inquiries on my XXXX report. 

Eagle Home Mortgage has indicated that it is their policy to pull a report from one of the bureaus to determine if the customer qualifies. After the initial review, they pull a report from all bureaus. This results in the consumer having a double inquiry for one of the bureaus. Consumers are not made aware that Eagle Home Mortgage will pull their report twice. 

I attempted to speak to someone about this for weeks. I left a message with multiple people, including my loan officer 's manager. I informed two of the loan officers and a rep at the company about the issue and they informed me that they would look into it. After weeks, I only got a reply after I contacted them again and threatened to file a formal complaint. Their response is that inquiries are only typically removed if there's an error. They followed up with claims that the second inquiry does not affect my score. They fail to realize that although the extra inquiry may not cause a drop in my score, the mere fact that it increased my total number of inquiries does affect my overall creditworthiness. They are also missing the point that I did not authorize them to pull my report multiple times. 

Eagle Home Mortgage should discontinue their practice of pulling consumers ' credit reports multiple times without their permission. When consumers provide permission to have their credit pulled, they have every reason to expect the company to only pull their information once and to seek permission for subsequent inquiries. I did not grant Eagle Home Mortgage the freedom to pull my credit as many times as they wish. I provided approval for one credit pull. So, one of the XXXX  inquiries should be removed.

consumer_complaint_narrative:
XXXX XXXX : Became aware that the CC was not being paid off as intended. 
XXXX XXXX : Called BofA ; held for ~25 min ( est. 4 min wait time ) Explained situation. Service rep. Agreed payment options confusing. 
Service rep. said refund request denied. 
I informed service rep Id be submitting complaints to relevant agencies. 
Rep said she would submit a complaint with BofA. 

Account opened : XXXX Bank of America Corporate Center XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, NC XXXX Submitted claim to Office of the Comptroller of the Currency : When I opened this account on XXXX XXXX, XXXX, I setup autopay. My intent was to pay off the entirety of the bill like I've done with 99 % of all statements for every credit card I've had for the past 20+ years. I've never intentionally left a balance on a CC ever. 

The options presented where objectively misleading. The four options were " Minimum Amount Due '', " Amount Due '', " Account Balance '', and " Fixed Amount ''. Given these options, I thought " Amount Due '' was clearly what was wanted as this would be the " amount due on the statement ''. And, by process of elimination, " Minimum Amount Due '' and " Fixed Amount '' were not that, and " Account Balance '' refers to the balance of the account at time of payment, and since only wanted to pay the statement balance, " Amount Due '' seemed the clear choice. 

However, seeing that the statements were not being paid off, I clicked the " help '' and it informed me that " Minimum Amount Due '' and " Amount Due '' are effectively the same option and that " Account Balance '' is ( it seems ) actually the " statement balance ''. Redefining a common term as something else and offering two options which are equivalent is at best confusing and, given the resources and knowledge of BofA, I assume intentionally misleading. 

After setting up auto-pay, I had logged in to ensure that a first payment was scheduled. Believing I was covered, I may have checked the account a few times, but didn't pay attention to the payments or balances since I was sure that I was paying off the balance. On XX/XX/XXXX, I became aware that this was not the case. I called BofA using the number on the back of the card. After explaining the situation, my request for a refund of the interest charges was denied. I informed the company I would be lodging complaints with the relevant agencies. 

The more common options, that I have seen ( confirmed with XXXX account ) are " Minimum Due '', " Statement Balance '', and " Fixed Amount ''. By using less clear, factually incorrect, and ultimately misleading options, BofA created enticed myself ( and I assume others ) to select the wrong option. I am requesting a refund of all interest payments and that BofA be advised to change their options to match standard terminology. 

Interest payments to date equal are {$150.00}. I have paid off the balance of the card, including interest fees, in order to mitigate further damage. I may incur additional interest depending on settlement and payment timing. This payment in no way represents a concession to BofA in this matter. 

Complaints submitted to BofA, OCC, CFPB, and XXXX.
